rationale: A wins because it knows the hard story is the collision of climate claim, cost cuts, and losses: "Oatly cuts the carbon footprint of its barista oat milk by 31% while closing a US plant." B has useful bones, but it repeatedly upgrades a supplier-default fact into category drama: "One coffee chain just made dairy optional. Dairy is taking notice." That line would get a founder into trouble; A's ugly questions would keep them out of it.
gaps_in_A: "A 1,400-store coffee chain makes oat milk the default, not the upcharge" overstates the update. The facts say default non-dairy option, not no surcharge and not dairy replacement.

"The prevailing belief is that unprofitable plant-based companies retreat from sustainability spending when they cut costs" is a sharp thesis, but the update does not provide evidence for that prevailing belief or for incremental sustainability spending.
"the same quarter delivers a verified footprint reduction and a plant closure" compresses timing. Before pitching, A needs exact dates for the reformulation, closure announcement, and quarterly loss.
gaps_in_B: "a chain-wide default switch away from dairy" is invented. The update says Oatly becomes the default non-dairy option, not that dairy stops being the default milk.
"When oat milk stops being the alternative and becomes the default pour" turns one regional chain fact into a category claim without the required second example or market data.
"Dairy is taking notice" fabricates reaction from an incumbent industry. No dairy source, trade-group response, displacement volume, or competitor signal appears in the update.
"five viable shapes exist here" is false generosity. At least two of those shapes are speculative enough to burn reporter trust before the founder gets to the real news.
